research_text:
# Research brief: MessageDigestSpec / `java.security.MessageDigest` / "expecting one of … but found SHA-1"

**Main limitation:** I could not retrieve the file at the raw.githubusercontent.com URL named in Q4. My tools could only search, not fetch a URL directly. The searches returned only the repository landing pages and papers that reproduce older versions of the rule. For Q4 I therefore cannot give a verbatim clause from the live file, and I have not reconstructed one.

## Q1. What `MessageDigest` governs, and what the finding refers to

- **What the class does.** The Javadoc says the class provides applications the functionality of a message digest algorithm, such as SHA-1 or SHA-256. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- **How an instance is obtained.** The JCA Reference Guide says instances are obtained by using one of the getInstance() methods in the MessageDigest class. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
  - `getInstance(String algorithm)` returns a MessageDigest object that implements the specified digest algorithm.
  - `getInstance(String, Provider)` is an overload that takes a provider.
- **What the finding refers to.** Reading the finding against the CrySL model, the "value" is the `algorithm` string argument of a `getInstance` factory call. The CrySL papers describe rules in which the `OBJECTS` section declares variables such as `algorithm` and the `EVENTS` section binds them to method parameters. The actual values of an event's parameters are assigned to the rule's variable names. Constraints are then evaluated on those values. Sources:
  - https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/
  - https://www.bodden.de/pubs/tse19CrySL.pdf
- **What the finding does not tell you.** Nothing in the Javadoc says whether the call site is a security use or a non-security use. That classification is not documented by the API.

## Q2. Documented correct and safe usage, and recommended remediation

- **Algorithm naming.** The Javadoc says the name should be a standard Java Security name (such as "SHA-256"). It points to the Standard Algorithm Names specification. The same specification states that standard names are not case-sensitive. Sources:
  - https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
  - https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- **Call sequence.**
  - `digest()` completes the hash computation, and the digest is reset after this call is made.
  - `digest(byte[])` first calls update(input), passing the input array to the update method, then calls digest().
  - A `digest(byte[])` call directly after `getInstance` is therefore documented API behavior.
  - Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- **Comparing digests.** `isEqual(byte[], byte[])` is documented only as comparing two digests for equality. The JDK 8 Javadoc describes it as a simple byte compare. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- **What the official JDK docs say about SHA-1.**
  - SHA-1 is listed as a supported algorithm and is not marked deprecated in the Javadoc I retrieved.
  - I found no `MessageDigest` Javadoc statement that SHA-1 is unsafe or that gives a remediation for it. This is a source limit, not a confirmed absence.
  - The JDK restricts SHA-1 only in specific subsystems through security properties. The JSSE guide lists `jdk.certpath.disabledAlgorithms` defaults that include MD2, MD5, SHA1 jdkCA & usage TLSServer, plus a SignedJAR restriction. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html
  - These properties govern TLS and certificate path checking and signed JARs. They do not govern direct `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` calls.
- **External standard.** NIST says it will transition away from the use of SHA-1 for applying cryptographic protection to all applications by December 31, 2030. NIST also notes that SP 800-131A deprecated SHA-1 for generating new digital signatures in 2011. Sources:
  - https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/12/nist-transitioning-away-sha-1-all-applications
  - https://csrc.nist.gov/news/2022/nist-transitioning-away-from-sha-1-for-all-apps
  - Both documents are about cryptographic protection. Neither is a `MessageDigest` API remediation rule.
- **Recommended remediation.** The `MessageDigest` documentation gives no remediation for using SHA-1. The only documented alternatives are the other standard names, which the JCA guide's samples illustrate with `"SHA-256"`.

## Q3. Compatibility when the algorithm is changed

- **Digest output differs by algorithm.** The Standard Names document says digest length ranges from 160 to 512 bits, depending on the algorithm. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html
  - Swapping the algorithm string therefore changes the output length and value.
  - Any persisted or on-the-wire value computed with SHA-1 would no longer match.
  - I found no official `MessageDigest` document that describes a migration path for persisted identifiers, wire formats or cache keys. This falls under your policy rule that those uses need separate migration evidence.
- **Platform version support.** The documents I retrieved disagree on which algorithms every implementation must support:
  - JDK 8: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html).
  - JDK 25: the "implementation requirements" row appears to list SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-384 (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html). The snippet is fragmentary, so I am not certain of it.
  - The SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 names appear in the JDK 8 Standard Names page. I did not verify the release in which they were introduced, or the status of SHA-3 names.
  - Implementations of the Java platform may vary in what else they provide. The OpenJDK source comment tells users to consult an implementation's release documentation. Source: https://github.com/openjdk/jdk/blob/35c4702055ccf11975391df01f62a70e06ecae83/src/java.base/share/classes/java/security/MessageDigest.java
- **Provider dependence.** The `getInstance(String, Provider)` Javadoc notes that the specified Provider does not have to be registered in the provider list. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- **Unresolved.** I found no official source on Android or Java ME compatibility for these algorithms. https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/MessageDigest appeared in results, but I did not read its algorithm table.

## Q4. What the CrySL rule applies

**Source status.** The master-branch file at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl was not retrieved, so no verbatim clause can be quoted from it.

**What I could verify from secondary sources:**

- **A published, older version of the rule.** The Bonifácio et al. paper reproduces the rule as SPEC java.security.MessageDigest. It has an event `g1: getInstance(algorithm);` and a constraint of the form `algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512", "BLAKE2B-512"}`. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04950
  - This copy differs from the three-algorithm set in your input, and the finding message lists six names (the three plus the hyphen-less SHA256, SHA384, SHA512).
  - I could not confirm which revision the detector bundles. Your input also says this is unknown.
- **Method names.**
  - In that published version, the event `g1` covers `getInstance` with one parameter, the `algorithm` string.
  - `u1` covers `update(_)`.
  - `d1` covers `digest()`.
  - The `_` wildcard is described as a placeholder for a parameter that need not be specified. Source: https://www.bodden.de/pubs/tse19CrySL.pdf
- **Receiver type.**
  - Each rule is a specification of one class, named in the `SPEC` clause, and the `EVENTS` block lists calls on objects of that class. Source: https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/
  - The TSE paper says events resolve to method signatures made of a method name and argument types. Source: https://www.bodden.de/pubs/tse19CrySL.pdf
- **Parameter list.**
  - In the CrySL syntax, a pattern such as `getInstance(algorithm)` states the parameters, and `_` marks a parameter that is left unconstrained.
  - The papers describe a pattern as covering the overloads that fit it. For `getInstance(String, …)`, the paper says the first pattern matches calls to `getInstance(String` and the overload with a second parameter.
  - So the pattern does constrain the parameter list, at least by argument count and types.
- **Same-name methods on other classes.**
  - From the secondary descriptions, a rule applies to the class named in `SPEC`, and events are resolved method signatures.
  - On that basis a same-named method on an unrelated class would not be matched.
  - This is inference from papers, not from the rule file. I cannot confirm it from the file or the analyzer's implementation.
- **Condition evaluated.** The finding message suggests set membership of the algorithm argument. Sources:
  - https://www.bodden.de/pubs/tse19CrySL.pdf
  - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04950
  - The membership constraint is the one shown in the published version above.
  - The condition is evaluated on the value the analysis resolves for the argument. An unresolved value is a behavior the rule file does not define, as your input also notes.

**Not verified:** the current file's exact clause text, whether it has `Update` or `Digest` event overloads beyond what the papers show, and the offset and length constraints your input describes. The CryptoAnalysis wiki shows a `TypestateError` listing `update` and `digest(byte[])` overloads for this class. Source: https://github.com/CROSSINGTUD/CryptoAnalysis/wiki/False-Positive,-False-Negatives-&-True-Positives

## Open questions

1. The exact text and revision of the live `MessageDigest.crysl` file, and the revision the detector bundles.
2. Whether the allowed set is three names or six. The detector message lists six; the supplied summary lists three.
3. The official guidance on migrating persisted or wire-format SHA-1 values. I found none.
4. Which JDK release added each SHA-2 variant. I did not confirm this.
